projects.name: Baptist Healthcare — Pine App
projects.summary: Redesigned five interconnected healthcare modules — PineApp mobile, Phressia Dashboard, Shopify Pharmacy, a Chatbot called PineApp Connect, and the Employee App.
projects.detail: The rethought appointment booking flow drove an 18% increase in patient bookings and reduced drop-off significantly. The project won four award categories. I used Claude and Figma Make to generate design system components 40% faster than traditional methods.
outcomes: Won 4 award categories including Mobile Website and Patient Portal
40% faster design system component creation using Claude + Figma Make

case_study.challenge: Baptist Healthcare was losing patients at the appointment booking stage. The existing PineApp had 5 interconnected systems (patient app, provider dashboard, pharmacy, chatbot, employee app) that weren't designed to work together. Drop-off rates were 40% — meaning 4 in 10 patients starting to book an appointment were abandoning the process. No cohesive design system existed.

research.key_findings: Patients were confused by multiple logins, unclear appointment availability display, and lack of confirmation messaging. Providers complained about scattered patient data across systems. The biggest drop-off was after selecting time — patients couldn't see the full appointment cost upfront.

case_study.strategy: Create a unified design system that treats all 5 touchpoints as one ecosystem. Redesign the appointment booking flow to show cost upfront, use progressive disclosure, and provide real-time confirmation. Build a shared component library to eliminate inconsistency.
case_study.design_approach: Atomic Design methodology — start with atoms (buttons, inputs), build molecules (date pickers, time slots), then organisms (full booking card, dashboard panels). Each component was designed for accessibility (WCAG 2.1 AA) and tested across iOS, Android, web, and internal systems.

team.structure: Me (UX Lead + Strategy), 2 interaction designers, 1 visual designer, 2 product managers, 1 researcher

key_decisions.decision: Made appointment cost visible immediately, not at checkout
key_decisions.reasoning: Data showed 35% of drop-offs happened at payment. Showing cost upfront eliminated the surprise factor and reduced cart abandonment by 22%.
key_decisions.trade_off: Meant redesigning the entire booking flow and negotiating pricing rules with the backend team.

key_decisions.decision: Used a unified login across all 5 apps
key_decisions.reasoning: Patient interviews showed frustration with multiple passwords. One login reduced friction and increased feature discovery.
key_decisions.trade_off: Required significant backend integration work — worth it for 18% booking increase.

key_decisions.decision: Used Claude + Figma Make to auto-generate component variants
key_decisions.reasoning: With 200+ design system components needed, manual design would take 6 weeks. Prompt-based generation cut it to 2 weeks.
key_decisions.trade_off: Required heavy QA and refinement — I spent 3 weeks auditing and adjusting the AI outputs.

case_study.design_methodology: Atomic Design, mobile-first, progressive disclosure, gestalt principles for visual hierarchy
case_study.ai_methodology: I wrote detailed component description prompts, fed them to Claude, and used the outputs as a starting template. Then I manually refined colors, spacing, and interaction states. This hybrid approach was 70% faster than pure manual design without compromising quality.
learnings: In healthcare, showing cost early builds trust even if it causes some drop-off — users prefer honesty to surprises.
A shared design system across 5 interconnected apps is worth the upfront investment; it pays back in consistency and team velocity.
AI is fastest when you have a clear rubric. Vague prompts create unusable outputs; detailed component briefs create 80% usable templates.
The appointment booking is the critical moment in healthcare UX — every 1% improvement here compounds into significant revenue.

projects.name: TAMM Conversational AI Design System
projects.summary: Built the component library and visual framework for a government-facing conversational AI platform.
projects.detail: One cohesive design system across all digital touchpoints — which meant users interacted with consistent, well-designed AI across every government service. The measurable outcome was a 35% drop in B2B manual support tickets. When conversational AI is designed properly, people self-serve more.
outcomes: 35% reduction in B2B manual support tickets
Scalable component library adopted across all touchpoints
Cohesive brand language across government AI services

case_study.challenge: TAMM (a UAE government AI platform) had 12+ government agencies using its conversational AI services, but each was implementing it differently. Inconsistent chatbot designs were confusing users and creating fragmented experiences. Support tickets were high because users didn't understand how to interact with the AI. There was no agreed-upon design language for how a government AI should 'feel.'

methods: Competitive analysis of enterprise AI platforms
Accessibility audit of existing AI interfaces
research.key_findings: Users didn't understand that they were talking to an AI (some thought they were chatting with humans). The chatbot's responses were inconsistent in tone and detail. Mobile experience was clunky — long response cards didn't reflow well. Users needed clear indicators of what the AI could and couldn't do.

case_study.strategy: Build a scalable Conversational AI Design System that makes it obvious you're talking to an AI while maintaining a professional government tone. Design for clarity, scannability, and progressive disclosure. Create reusable patterns for common queries (FAQs, forms, escalation).
case_study.design_approach: Conversational Design + Systems Thinking. First, I defined AI personality (professional, accurate, empathetic). Then I built patterns: greeting cards, response bubbles with metadata, quick-reply suggestions, escalation paths, empty states. Each pattern was designed to work on mobile, tablet, and desktop.

team.structure: Me (Design System Lead), 3 conversation designers, 2 UX researchers, 4 product managers (one per agency), 2 engineers

case_study.timeline: 5 months from kickoff to adoption across all agencies

key_decisions.decision: Made it explicit that users were talking to an AI, not a human
key_decisions.reasoning: Some users felt deceived when they realized. Being transparent from the start built trust and set correct expectations.
key_decisions.trade_off: Some users initially preferred the illusion of human contact, but support tickets dropped 35% once expectations were clear.

key_decisions.decision: Designed quick-reply suggestions instead of free-text input for complex queries
key_decisions.reasoning: Government agencies had high accuracy requirements. Guided interactions reduced misunderstandings and improved first-contact resolution.
key_decisions.trade_off: Less user freedom, but better outcomes — users adapted within 2 weeks.

key_decisions.decision: Built escalation pathways into the design, not the backend
key_decisions.reasoning: Making 'talk to a human' obvious reduced support anxiety and increased feature adoption. Users felt safer trying the AI.
key_decisions.trade_off: Required alignment with 12 agency staffing models — took 2 weeks of stakeholder negotiation.

case_study.design_methodology: Conversational Design (Moore & Moran), Card-Based UI patterns, Progressive Disclosure, Accessibility-First
case_study.governance: Created a 'Design System RFC' process where each agency could propose variations, but all had to start from the system. This maintained consistency while allowing for agency-specific needs.
learnings: Conversational AI needs visual scaffolding — users need help understanding the bounds of what the AI can do.
Governments require a different tone than consumer apps; authority and accuracy build trust, not personality.
The most powerful feature of good conversational design is clarity about what happens next.
Support ticket reduction is a leading indicator of design quality in AI systems — when users understand how to interact, they self-serve.
Scaling a design system across 12 stakeholders requires governance, not just documentation.
